blocks.text: Switching a 500 MW power station from coal to natural gas cuts its carbon dioxide emission per kilowatt-hour by more than half, and switching again from a 35 per cent to a 55 per cent efficient plant cuts it by another third; but the gas plant may cost more per kilowatt-hour to run, depending on fuel price. Engineers must put numbers on both sides before a decision. This unit gives the tools: carbon intensity, levelised cost, and a structured comparison.

blocks.markdown: **Carbon intensity** is the mass of CO$_2$ emitted per unit of useful energy. It follows from three things: the carbon content of the fuel, its heating value and the efficiency of conversion. When a fuel burns completely, each kilogram of carbon becomes $44/12=3.667$ kg of CO$_2$, because the molar masses are 44 g/mol for CO$_2$ and 12 g/mol for carbon (oxygen added from the air).

blocks.title: Carbon intensity of electricity
blocks.text: For a fuel with carbon mass fraction $c$ and lower heating value $LHV$ (MJ/kg), burned in a plant of efficiency $\eta$, the CO$_2$ emitted per kWh of electricity is $e=\dfrac{3.6}{\eta\,LHV}\,c\,\dfrac{44}{12}$ kg/kWh. The factor 3.6 MJ/kWh converts energy units. The **fuel emission factor** is $c\times44/12/LHV$ in kg per MJ of fuel.

blocks.caption: CO2 per kWh of electricity (LHV in MJ/kg; carbon complete combustion)

blocks.title: Carbon intensity of gas and coal plants
blocks.prompt: Natural gas (treat as methane, carbon fraction $c=0.75$, typical $LHV=50$ MJ/kg) in a combined-cycle plant of efficiency 0.55, against a coal (typical $c=0.7$, $LHV=28$ MJ/kg) plant of efficiency 0.38. Find the CO$_2$ per kWh of electricity for each.

steps.text: Fuel energy per kWh of electricity.

blocks.answer: The gas plant emits about 0.36 kg CO$_2$/kWh and the coal plant about 0.868 kg/kWh, a ratio of about 2.4.

blocks.caption: Carbon intensity from fuel and efficiency (values illustrative)

blocks.markdown: **Levelised cost of energy (LCOE).** The LCOE is the constant price per kWh that recovers all lifetime costs. The capital cost $C$ (per kW) is converted to an annual charge by the **capital recovery factor** $CRF=i(1+i)^n/[(1+i)^n-1]$ for discount rate $i$ and life $n$ years. Fixed operating costs add per kW-year. Dividing by the annual energy output per kW, $8760\,CF$ kWh where $CF$ is the capacity factor, gives the cost per kWh. Fuel cost per kWh is the fuel price per MJ times $3.6/\eta$, and variable O&M adds directly.

blocks.caption: LCOE per kWh; p_fuel in currency per MJ; C and fixed O&M per kW (per kW-year)

blocks.title: LCOE of a gas plant
blocks.prompt: A gas-fired plant costs USD 900 per kW, discount rate 8%, life 25 years, fixed O&M USD 25 per kW-year, capacity factor 0.6. Fuel costs USD 8 per GJ with plant efficiency 0.55, and variable O&M is USD 0.003 per kWh. Find the LCOE.

steps.text: Capital recovery factor and annual capital charge.
Annual energy per kW and the capital plus fixed cost per kWh.
Fuel cost per kWh: $\text{US\$8/GJ}=\text{US\$0.008/MJ}$ times fuel energy per kWh.

blocks.answer: The LCOE is about USD 0.0762 per kWh, of which fuel is about 68.8%.

blocks.title: Comparing the options with a carbon price
blocks.prompt: For the gas and coal plants above, a carbon price of USD 50 per tonne CO$_2$ is introduced. Find the added cost per kWh for each.

steps.text: Cost per kWh is emission per kWh times price per kg (USD 50/t = USD 0.05/kg).

blocks.answer: A USD 50/t carbon price adds about USD 0.018/kWh to gas and USD 0.0434/kWh to coal, so it narrows or reverses any cost advantage of the dirtier plant.

items: Tabulate each option's efficiency, carbon intensity (kg CO$_2$/kWh) and LCOE (cost per kWh) on the same basis.
Identify what drives each metric: fuel carbon and efficiency for emissions; capital, capacity factor and fuel price for cost.
Test sensitivity: vary the discount rate, capacity factor, fuel price and carbon price one at a time.
Present the trade-off and a break-even (for example the carbon price at which two options cost the same) rather than a single winner.

blocks.title: LCOE depends strongly on capacity factor and discount rate
blocks.text: Capital-intensive options (wind, solar, nuclear) have most of their cost in the capital term $(C\cdot CRF)/(8760\,CF)$, so a lower capacity factor or a higher discount rate raises their LCOE sharply. Fuel-intensive options (gas, coal) are more exposed to the fuel price and, increasingly, the carbon price. A fair comparison states $i$, $n$ and $CF$ explicitly.

points: CO$_2$ per kWh$_e$: $e=(3.6/\eta)\,c\,(44/12)/LHV$; higher efficiency and lower-carbon fuel reduce it.
LCOE: annualised capital plus fixed O&M over annual energy, plus fuel cost $3.6p/\eta$ and variable O&M.
Compare options on efficiency, emissions and cost together; use sensitivity and break-even carbon prices.

questions.stem: Complete combustion of 1.00 kg of carbon in air produces what mass of carbon dioxide?

options.text: 3.67 kg, because the molar mass ratio of CO$_2$ to carbon is 44/12
1.00 kg, because mass is conserved in the fuel
2.67 kg, because only the oxygen mass is counted
1.83 kg, because CO$_2$ contains half carbon by moles

questions.correctOptionText: 3.67 kg, because the molar mass ratio of CO$_2$ to carbon is 44/12

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the product mass is 44/12 times the carbon mass.
distractorRationale.b: The oxygen from the air adds mass; the fuel mass alone is not conserved in the product.
distractorRationale.c: Counts only the added oxygen and omits the carbon.
distractorRationale.d: Mixes moles and mass: the mass ratio is 44/12, not 44/24.

questions.explanation: Each carbon atom (12 g/mol) combines with an O$_2$ molecule (32 g/mol) to give CO$_2$ (44 g/mol). The mass of CO$_2$ is therefore $44/12=3.67$ times the mass of carbon burned.

questions.stem: For the same fuel, a power station improves its efficiency from 35% to 45%. The CO$_2$ emitted per kWh of electricity changes by a factor of:

distractorRationale.a: Inverts the ratio; efficiency improvement cannot increase emissions per kWh.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: emissions per kWh scale as one over the efficiency.
distractorRationale.c: Subtracts the efficiencies, which is not a proportional relationship.
distractorRationale.d: Assumes emissions depend only on the fuel, not on how much electricity it yields.

questions.explanation: Emission per kWh is inversely proportional to efficiency, so the ratio is $0.35/0.45=0.778$, a 22 per cent reduction. The fuel carbon is the same, but less fuel is burned per kWh.

questions.stem: For a capital-intensive power plant (high capital cost, no fuel cost), raising the discount rate from 5% to 10%, with everything else unchanged, will:

options.text: lower the LCOE, because future costs are discounted more heavily
leave the LCOE unchanged, because the capital cost is fixed
raise the LCOE, because the capital recovery factor increases
raise only the fuel component, because fuel is bought annually

questions.correctOptionText: raise the LCOE, because the capital recovery factor increases

distractorRationale.a: The annualised capital charge rises with the discount rate, which dominates for such plants.
distractorRationale.b: The financing cost depends on the rate, through the capital recovery factor.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: a higher discount rate increases the capital recovery factor.
distractorRationale.d: This plant has no fuel cost, and the discount rate acts on capital.

questions.explanation: The capital recovery factor $i(1+i)^n/[(1+i)^n-1]$ grows with $i$, so the annual capital charge rises. In a capital-dominated plant, this raises the LCOE nearly in proportion.

questions.stem: A wind farm's capacity factor falls from 40% to 20% because of a calmer site. If capital and fixed costs dominate, its LCOE roughly:

options.text: halves, because fewer hours of operation cost less
is unchanged, because the capital cost is unchanged
increases by 20%, because the difference in capacity factors is 20 percentage points
doubles, because the same annual cost is spread over half the energy

questions.correctOptionText: doubles, because the same annual cost is spread over half the energy

distractorRationale.a: Costs are largely fixed; they do not scale with the energy produced.
distractorRationale.b: Per-kWh cost is the annual cost divided by the energy, which has halved.
distractorRationale.c: The relevant ratio is 40 to 20, a factor of two, not the percentage-point difference.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: fixed annual costs are divided by half as much energy.

questions.explanation: The cost per kWh is $(C\cdot CRF+O\&M)/(8760\,CF)$. Halving $CF$ halves the annual energy in the denominator, so the LCOE roughly doubles when capital and fixed cost dominate.

questions.stem: Plant A has a lower LCOE but a higher CO$_2$ intensity than plant B. A government introduces a carbon price. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The cost of plant A rises by more per kWh than that of plant B, so the cost gap narrows and may reverse at a high enough price
Both plants' costs rise by the same amount per kWh
Plant B's cost rises more, since it is more expensive
The carbon price has no effect on the ranking, because LCOE already includes all costs

questions.correctOptionText: The cost of plant A rises by more per kWh than that of plant B, so the cost gap narrows and may reverse at a high enough price

distractorRationale.a: Correct: carbon cost scales with each plant's emission per kWh.
distractorRationale.b: The added cost is proportional to each plant's own emission per kWh.
distractorRationale.c: The carbon cost depends on emissions, not on the base cost.
distractorRationale.d: A carbon price adds a new cost, proportional to emissions, to the LCOE.

questions.explanation: The added cost per kWh equals emission per kWh times the carbon price, so the higher-emission plant A is penalised more. The break-even price is the cost difference divided by the emission difference.

questions.stem: A diesel-fired power plant burns fuel oil with carbon mass fraction 0.86 and LHV 42 MJ/kg, at an electrical efficiency of 0.40. Using 44/12 for the CO$_2$ to carbon mass ratio, find the CO$_2$ emitted per kWh of electricity in kg/kWh.
questions.explanation: Fuel energy per kWh$_e$ is $3.6/0.40=9.0$ MJ, so the fuel burned is $9.0/42=0.2143$ kg. Carbon in it is $0.2143\times0.86$ kg, giving CO$_2$ of $0.1843\times3.667=0.6757$ kg/kWh.

questions.stem: A solar farm costs USD 1000 per kW, with a 6% discount rate, a 25-year life, fixed O&M of USD 15 per kW-year, no fuel and a capacity factor of 0.20. Find the LCOE in USD  per kWh.
questions.explanation: $CRF=0.06\times1.06^{25}/(1.06^{25}-1)=0.07823$, so the capital charge is $1000\times0.07823=78.23$ USD /kW-yr. With O&M the annual cost is $93.23$ USD /kW-yr, and the energy is $8760\times0.20=1752$ kWh/kW-yr, so the LCOE is $0.05321$ USD /kWh.

questions.stem: Plant A has an LCOE of USD 0.058/kWh and emits 0.80 kg CO$_2$/kWh. Plant B has an LCOE of USD 0.071/kWh and emits 0.37 kg CO$_2$/kWh. Find the carbon price in USD  per tonne of CO$_2$ at which the two plants have the same total cost per kWh.
questions.explanation: Set $0.058+0.80p=0.071+0.37p$ with $p$ in USD /kg. Then $p=(0.071-0.058)/(0.80-0.37)=0.013/0.43=0.03023$ USD /kg, which is 30.23 USD  per tonne. Above this price plant B is cheaper overall.

questions.stem: Two options for supplying 100 MW are a gas combined-cycle plant and a wind farm with battery storage. Explain how you would compare them on efficiency, emissions and cost, and why a single metric such as LCOE alone is insufficient.
markingGuide: Efficiency: conversion efficiency of the gas plant (fuel to electricity) versus capacity factor and system efficiency including storage losses for wind
Emissions: gas carbon intensity from fuel carbon, LHV and efficiency (kg per kWh) versus near-zero operating emissions for wind, plus embodied emissions
Cost: LCOE from capital recovery, fixed and variable O&M, and fuel (gas); sensitive to fuel price; wind capital dominated and sensitive to capacity factor and discount rate
Include a carbon price or break-even carbon price to link cost and emissions
LCOE ignores dispatchability, storage and grid integration cost, reliability and fuel-price risk
Concludes with a multi-criteria comparison and sensitivity analysis rather than one number
questions.explanation: A fair comparison reports all three metrics on the same basis and tests sensitivity. LCOE omits system effects such as the value of dispatchable supply and the cost of storage or backup, and it does not capture emissions unless a carbon price is added.

questions.stem: Outline the steps to calculate (a) the CO$_2$ emitted per kWh of electricity from a fuel's carbon content, its heating value and the plant efficiency, and (b) the levelised cost of energy of the plant. State the assumptions.
markingGuide: (a) Fuel energy per kWh electrical = 3.6/eta MJ
CO2 mass = fuel mass x carbon fraction x 44/12 (complete combustion)
(b) Annual capital charge = capital x CRF with CRF = i(1+i)^n/((1+i)^n - 1)
Add fixed O&M and divide by annual energy 8760 x CF per kW; add fuel cost 3.6 p/eta and variable O&M
Assumptions: complete combustion, constant efficiency and prices, constant discount rate and life, no inflation or taxes
questions.explanation: Part (a) is a chain: electricity to fuel energy through the efficiency, fuel energy to fuel mass through the heating value, and fuel mass to carbon dioxide through the carbon fraction and 44/12. Part (b) annualises capital with the capital recovery factor, adds fixed cost, divides by annual output and adds the per-kWh fuel and variable costs.
